borders.before: welcome, introduction of lecturers, course context, and lecture learning outcomes
borders.after: fundamental definitions of cancer as a genetic and evolutionary disease, microenvironment, and risk
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is administrative and framing introductory material, whereas Subtopic 2 begins the substantive content explaining cancer biology.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no adjacent subtopic that serves framing purposes.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would conflate introductory framing with core biology concepts.

borders.before: epidemiological global variations, migrant studies, and genetic versus environmental risk balances
borders.after: involvement of specific infectious pathogens (bacteria, helminths, fungi, viruses) in carcinogenesis
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 2–6 discuss general concepts of cancer etiology, the 'roulette wheel' of internal/external causes, and epidemiology, whereas Subtopic 7 starts the systematic breakdown of specific classes of environmental carcinogens, beginning with infectious agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving earlier to 6 would split the broad epidemiological framing from the general discussion of causes.
borders.caseForRemoving: Pathogen mechanisms form a distinct, specific thematic section compared to the broad introductory framing of cancer causes.

borders.before: Burkitt lymphoma history, epidemiology, malaria connection, and EBV/Myc translocation mechanisms
borders.after: dietary mutagens like aflatoxin and the biochemical formation of DNA adducts
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 7-8 focus specifically on infectious agents (viruses, bacteria, parasites), whereas Subtopic 9 transitions to dietary and chemical carcinogens and their chemical mechanisms.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 8 concludes the infectious pathogen discussion with the Burkitt lymphoma case study.
borders.caseForRemoving: Chemical and physical mutagens involve distinct biochemical mechanisms (metabolic activation, adducts, UV dimers) separate from viral/microbial pathogenesis.

borders.before: aromatic amines (beta-naphthylamine) and tissue-specific metabolic activation
borders.after: asbestos, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between tumor initiators and promoters
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 shifts conceptually from direct mutagenic chemical adducts to non-mutagenic tumor promoters, chronic inflammation, and permissive microenvironments.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is strictly about metabolic activation of carcinogens (initiators/mutagens), while 14 begins non-mutagenic promoters.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would merge direct DNA mutagens with the classic initiator/promoter paradigm and host developmental susceptibility.

borders.before: summary of direct mutagens, promoters, and host developmental timing
borders.after: mutational signatures and high-throughput sequencing methods to identify carcinogen exposure
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 concludes the mechanistic overview of carcinogens, while Subtopic 18 initiates the experimental and analytical methods for identifying and proving carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 is explicitly a summary of the preceding etiology concepts.
borders.caseForRemoving: The methodologies (signatures, epidemiology, animal bioassays, Ames test) form a distinct pedagogical unit corresponding to a learning objective stated at the start.

borders.before: the Ames test, in vitro mutagenicity testing, and limitations of laboratory assays
borders.after: lecture wrap-up, perspective on risk-benefit trade-offs, and final summary
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 serves as the closing framing of the lecture, summarizing key takeaways and concluding remarks before audience applause.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 contains detailed scientific discussion of the Ames test, while 22 is purely conclusion and wrap-up.
borders.caseForRemoving: Standard lecture closing framing should stand as its own closing topic.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2-3 define cancer as a genetic/evolutionary process with endogenous and environmental mutations, whereas 4-6 review known environmental exposures and epidemiological studies across populations.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2–6 together build the general conceptual model of cancer etiology (bad luck, intrinsic mutations, environmental factors, and epidemiology) before drilling down into specific agent classes.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 introduces various infectious agents broadly, while Subtopic 8 is a deep dive into the Burkitt lymphoma case study.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 directly illustrates and expands upon the concepts of viral oncogenesis and pathogen interactions introduced in Subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9-10 cover aflatoxin and UV light, whereas 11-13 focus extensively on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and xenobiotic metabolism.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All subtopics (9–13) share the single focused theme of physical and chemical mutagens causing DNA adducts and mutations via metabolic activation or radiation.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14-15 focus on promotion versus initiation, while 16-17 discuss host life stage susceptibility and summarize.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14–17 collectively address non-mutagenic/host-dependent factors in carcinogenesis (promoters, inflammation, host developmental stage) and conclude with a synthesis summary.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 discusses sequencing mutational signatures, whereas 19-21 cover epidemiological biobanks, in vivo animal testing, and the in vitro Ames test.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All four subtopics systematically walk through the methodologies used to detect and prove carcinogenicity across sequencing, epidemiology, in vivo models, and in vitro assays.

topics.label: Introduction and Learning Outcomes
topics.groupedBecause: The lecture opens with introductory framing, lecturer introductions, and the outline of learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetics, Chance, and Environmental Exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics introduce cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease shaped by endogenous mutation rates, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns.

topics.label: Infectious Agents in Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the role of pathogens in cancer, focusing on mechanisms and the case study of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Chemical and Physical Mutagenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how physical radiation and chemical carcinogens undergo metabolic activation to induce DNA adducts and mutations.

topics.label: Tumor Promotion, Inflammation, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics analyze non-mutagenic promoters, chronic inflammation, and host developmental timing that facilitate cancer development.

topics.label: Methodologies for Determining Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics survey analytical, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro experimental approaches used to determine carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Perspective
topics.groupedBecause: The lecture concludes with a closing synthesis of environmental carcinogenesis and the risk-benefit trade-offs of daily exposures.
